I get asked this a lot: "How to you decide if you should build this in Copilot Studio or in Azure AI Foundry?" And my honest first answer is always "it depends," which helps nobody. So here's how I actually think it through.The short versionCopilot Studio is for building an agent quickly, low-code, that talks to people in Teams, on a website, or inside M365 Copilot. Foundry is for when you're building AI into something more custom, a product, a pipeline, whatever, and you want control over the model and the code around it.If the person using this thing is a business user asking questions and getting stuff done in Microsoft 365, go Copilot Studio. If it's a developer wiring a model into an app with logic that doesn't fit neatly into a conversation flow, go Foundry.That's the short version anyway. Like most short versions it falls apart a bit once you get into real projects.What Copilot Studio is good at- The visual builder for conversation flows (topics, triggers, generative answers) is genuinely fast once you get used to it- Connectors into Microsoft 365, Dataverse, and a long list of other services through Power Platform- Generative orchestration, so the agent can figure out which tool or knowledge source to use instead of you mapping every single path- Publishing to Teams, a website, or as an agent inside M365 Copilot is basically a couple of clicks- Auth and permissions mostly just work because it rides on Entra ID and the Power Platform security modelWhere it runs out of road: anything that needs real custom code beyond what a Power Automate flow can do, fine-grained control over the model itself (temperature, raw system prompts), or you're calling this thing constantly from your own backend at volume.What Foundry is good at- Direct access to the model catalog: Azure OpenAI models, Meta, Mistral, others depending on region, with full control over parameters and streaming- An actual dev setup: SDKs for Python, C#, JS, prompt flow, evaluation tools, tracing- Content safety you can tune properly (I wrote a separate post on that, it's its own rabbit hole)- Room to build real custom orchestration: multi-step agents, tool calling, your own RAG setup, stuff that doesn't map onto Copilot Studio's topic model cleanly- Works in any app, not just inside Microsoft 365Where it runs out of road: getting something in front of business users fast, without writing code. Foundry assumes there's a developer involved somewhere. Copilot Studio doesn't.The questions I actually ask myself1. Who's using this: a person in Teams/a browser, or a system/developer? First one, Copilot Studio. Second, Foundry.2. Is there a developer on this project at all? If not, Foundry's not really on the table.3. Does this fit a conversation-and-tools pattern, or does it need real custom logic? Conversation pattern, Copilot Studio handles it. Custom logic, you need Foundry somewhere in the stack, even if it's just the backend.4. Where does this need to show up: Teams, M365 Copilot, a simple web widget? Copilot Studio. A mobile app, a product, a backend service? Foundry.
